chunks.text: The bottle palm is endemic to tiny Round Island, off the coast of Mauritius, and is one of only two Hyophorbe species still surviving there in the wild (the other, Hyophorbe vaughanii, is itself critically endangered). Its defining trait is a dramatically swollen trunk that bulges near the base before tapering upward — a shape sometimes described as 'bizarre' — which, contrary to popular belief repeated in some gardening sources, Wikipedia notes is not actually a water-storage adaptation; this swelling pattern is also what distinguishes it from the similarly bottle-shaped spindle palm, whose trunk swells in the middle rather than near the base. The palm typically carries only four to six open leaves at a time, each emerging reddish or orange-tinted before maturing to a deep green, and its multi-branched inflorescences emerge from beneath the crownshaft, producing small orange or black fruit around 2.5 cm across. The IUCN's assessment (dating to 1998) rates it Critically Endangered, with ongoing habitat degradation threatening to wipe out the last wild individuals on Round Island entirely. Remarkably, the species' continued existence is now essentially guaranteed by horticulture rather than by its native population: it has been planted so extensively as an ornamental specimen across the tropics and subtropics that cultivated stock far outnumbers — and effectively backstops — what remains in the wild.

chunks.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Hyophorbe lagenicaulis (FR307)
chunks.text: The UF/IFAS fact sheet on the bottle palm describes a slow-growing palm typically 12–20 feet tall, native more broadly to the Mascarene Islands east of Madagascar, with pinnate fronds around 12 feet long whose slender, dark-green leaflets grow in opposite pairs along the rachis to form a visible V-shape. It details the trunk's development: young plants start with a swollen base that becomes progressively more elongated and less pronounced with age, eventually yielding the mature 'bottle' silhouette, all capped by a smooth, waxy, bright green crownshaft 2–3 feet tall. The sheet recommends full sun with tolerance for moderate shade, well-drained sandy soils reflecting its native upland-forest and coastal-savanna habitat, and extra irrigation through dry spells, while warning that freezing temperatures will most likely kill the palm outright — which is why, in the continental United States, it is realistically only recommended for south Florida and parts of coastal/southern California, alongside Hawaii. In Florida specifically, supplemental potassium fertilisation is advised to prevent the nutrient deficiencies that commonly afflict ornamental palms. As a landscape plant it is prized as a singular focal specimen or massed in small groups of three or more, and it can also be grown indoors given adequate light and headroom — though the sheet reiterates that in its natural range the species is critically endangered and close to extinction.
